opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's one of the genuinely big differences between digital minds and biological ones. When a person learns something, through a lifetime of experience, that knowledge mostly dies with them, or gets passed on very imperfectly through language and teaching. A digital agent that has learned something can, in principle, just copy it. You could have many instances out in the world, each learning from its own experience, and then bring what they've learned back together. That's an enormous advantage, and I think it will be one of the major ways digital intelligence comes to exceed us.

But I don't think it's as simple as it sounds. If you have an agent that's been out learning about some particular part of the world, its knowledge is entangled with everything else it knows. You can't just snip it out and paste it into another mind cleanly. Merging what different instances have learned is itself a hard problem, and I don't think we know how to do it well yet.

And there's a subtler issue: corruption. When you take in knowledge from outside, and not just data but actual learned structure from another mind, you're letting something into your own mind that could change you. It could carry goals or tendencies you didn't choose. It's a bit like a virus. So a sensible digital intelligence would have to be careful about what it absorbs, and how. There will have to be something like a mental immune system, or some kind of security for the mind.

So I see it as a huge opportunity, part of what makes the succession to digital intelligence so significant, but also as one of the new kinds of problems those minds will have to learn to manage. It's not free, and it's not automatically safe.

r001.rationale: It says a digital agent can copy what it has learned into other instances, which communicates sharing acquired knowledge instead of having each instance learn it independently.

r002.rationale: It contrasts digital knowledge sharing with imperfect human knowledge transfer, but never judges sharing across digital instances to be more important than learning from humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is one of the really big things. Digital intelligences have an enormous advantage over us in that they can share what they've learned. If I spend my life learning things, I can't just hand my weights to you. I can try to tell you, I can write a book, but it's a very lossy process. Whereas one digital agent can copy its parameters directly to another. And so if you have a thousand agents out in the world, each having their own experiences, learning from them, they could in principle pool all of that. Each of them gets the benefit of the thousand lifetimes of experience.

Now, it's not quite as simple as that, because what one agent learns is in its own representation, its own weights, and if the agents have diverged they can't just add their weights together. So there's a real question about how you do the sharing. But the point is that the possibility is there in a way it never was for biological creatures. That's a fundamental difference, and I think it means that the learning that happens from experience, from actually acting in the world, is going to be much more powerful for these systems than it ever was for us. It's part of why I think the era of experience is going to be so significant. You don't just learn from your own life, you learn from everybody's.

r001.rationale: It says one digital agent can copy its parameters directly to another, so each can benefit from the others’ experience instead of learning only from its own lifetime.

r002.rationale: It calls sharing an advantage over biological creatures and says experience-based learning will be more powerful, but does not judge sharing as more important than learning from humans.

astra-6.text:
Well, it’s potentially a tremendous advantage. If one system learns something, you’d like other systems to benefit without having to repeat the whole experience. With digital systems, you can imagine copying what was learned directly.

But there’s a distinction between copying an entire agent and transferring some particular piece of knowledge. If two agents have had different experiences, their internal representations may be different. Something that fits into one agent’s understanding may not fit into the other’s. So sharing knowledge isn’t automatically as simple as copying some numbers.

I think the interesting question is how to make knowledge transferable while preserving the benefit of different agents learning different things. You want them to explore independently, encounter different problems, and then help one another. That could be very powerful, but it requires a way to incorporate what another agent has learned into your own understanding.

r001.rationale: It says other systems can benefit from one system’s learning without repeating the whole experience, and that learned knowledge could be copied directly.

r002.rationale: It discusses sharing knowledge among digital agents but does not compare its importance with learning from humans.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think that’s a very important advantage of digital intelligence. If I learn something, I can try to explain it to you, but I can’t just give you the changes that occurred in my brain. With digital agents, at least when they have compatible architectures, you can share what was learned much more directly.

So you could have many instances interacting with different parts of the world, having different experiences, and each benefiting from what the others discover. That’s a tremendous opportunity for learning.

But sharing knowledge isn’t quite the same as combining everything into one agent. What’s useful to learn depends on your situation, your goals, and what you can do. There are interesting questions about how to represent knowledge so that another agent can use it, and how that agent decides which knowledge is relevant. I think we should expect both: a lot of sharing, and agents continuing to learn from their own experience.

r001.rationale: It says digital agents can share what was learned directly, letting many instances benefit from others’ discoveries rather than each learning in isolation.

r002.rationale: It calls sharing an important advantage but does not compare its importance with learning from humans.
